Definitions of Non-GAAP and other Key Financial Measures System-Wide Sales are neither required by, nor presented in accordance with, GAAP. System-wide sales are the sum of company-operated restaurant revenue and sales from franchise-operated restaurants. The Company’s total revenue in the consolidated statements of income is limited to company-operated restaurant revenue and franchise revenue from the Company’s franchisees. Accordingly, system-wide sales should not be considered in isolation or as a substitute for our results as reported under GAAP. Management believes that the presentation of system-wide sales provides useful information to investors, because it is a measure that is widely used in the restaurant industry, including by our management, to evaluate brand scale and market penetration. System-wide sales do not include the eight currently licensed stores in the Philippines. The total number of currently licensed stores reflects the closure of two licensed restaurants during the fiscal year ended December 31, 2025. Company-Operated Restaurant Revenue consists of sales of food and beverages in company-operated restaurants net of promotional allowances, employee meals, and other discounts. Company-operated restaurant revenue in any period is directly influenced by the number of operating weeks in such period, the number of open restaurants, and comparable restaurant sales. Seasonal factors and the timing of holidays cause our revenue to fluctuate from quarter to quarter. Our revenue per restaurant is typically lower in the first and fourth quarters due to reduced January and December transactions and higher in the second and third quarters. As a result of seasonality, our quarterly and annual results of operations and key performance indicators such as company-operated restaurant revenue and comparable restaurant sales may fluctuate. Comparable Restaurant Sales reflect year-over-year sales changes for comparable company-operated, franchise-operated and system-wide restaurants. A restaurant enters our comparable restaurant base the first full week after it has operated for 15 months. Comparable restaurant sales exclude restaurants closed during the applicable period. At July 1, 2026, there were 489 system-wide comparable restaurants, 172 company-operated restaurants and 317 franchise-operated restaurants. Comparable restaurant sales indicate the performance of existing restaurants, since new restaurants are excluded. Comparable restaurant sales growth can be generated by an increase in the number of meals sold and/or by increases in the average check amount, resulting from a shift in menu mix and/or higher prices resulting from new products or price increases. Because other companies may calculate this measure differently than we do, comparable restaurant sales as presented herein may not be comparable to similarly titled measures reported by other companies. Management believes that comparable restaurant sales is a valuable metric for investors to evaluate the performance of our store base, excluding the impact of new stores and closed stores. Restaurant Contribution and Restaurant Contribution Margin are neither required by, nor presented in accordance with, GAAP. Restaurant contribution is defined as company-operated restaurant revenue less company restaurant expenses, which includes food and paper cost, labor and related expenses, and occupancy and other operating expenses, where applicable. Restaurant contribution therefore excludes franchise revenue, franchise advertising fee revenue and franchise expenses as well as certain other costs, such as general and administrative expenses, depreciation and amortization, impairment and closed-store reserve, loss on disposal of assets and other costs that are considered corporate-level expenses and are not considered normal operating costs of our restaurants. Accordingly, restaurant contribution is not indicative of overall Company results and does not accrue directly to the benefit of stockholders because of the exclusion of certain corporate-level expenses. Restaurant contribution margin is defined as restaurant contribution as a percentage of company-operated restaurant revenue. Restaurant contribution and restaurant contribution margin are supplemental measures of operating performance of our restaurants, and our calculations thereof may not be comparable to those reported by other companies. Restaurant contribution and restaurant contribution margin have limitations as analytical tools, and you should not consider them in isolation, or superior to, or as substitutes for the analysis of our results as reported under GAAP. Management uses restaurant contribution and restaurant contribution margin as key metrics to evaluate the profitability of incremental sales at our restaurants, to evaluate our restaurant performance across periods, and to evaluate our restaurant financial performance compared with our competitors. Management believes that restaurant contribution and restaurant contribution margin are important tools for investors, because they are widely-used metrics within the restaurant industry to evaluate restaurant-level productivity, efficiency, and performance. Management further believes restaurant level operating margin is useful to investors to highlight trends in our core business that may not otherwise be apparent to investors when relying solely on GAAP financial measures. EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA are neither required by, nor presented in accordance with, GAAP. EBITDA represents net income (loss) before interest expense, provision (benefit) for income taxes, depreciation, and amortization, and Adjusted EBITDA represents net income (loss) before interest expense (net of interest income), provision (benefit) for income taxes, depreciation, amortization, and items that we do not consider representative of our ongoing operating performance, as identified in the reconciliation table included under “Unaudited Reconciliation of Net Income to EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA” in the accompanying financial tables at the end of this release. EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA as presented in this release are supplemental measures of our performance that are neither required by, nor presented in accordance with, GAAP. EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA are not measurements of our financial performance under GAAP and should not be considered as alternatives to net income, operating income, or any other performance measures derived in accordance with GAAP, or as alternatives to cash flow from operating activities as a measure of our liquidity. In addition, in evaluating EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA, you should be aware that in the future we will incur expenses or charges such as those added back to calculate EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA. Our presentation of EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA should not be construed as an inference that our future results will be unaffected by unusual or nonrecurring items. EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA have limitations as analytical tools, and you should not consider them in isolation, or as substitutes for analysis of our results as reported under GAAP. Some of these limitations are (i) they do not reflect our cash expenditures, or future requirements for capital expenditures or contractual commitments, (ii) they do not reflect changes in, or cash requirements for, our working capital needs, (iii) they do not reflect the significant interest expense, or the cash requirements necessary to service interest or principal payments, on our debt, (iv) although depreciation and amortization are non-cash charges, the assets being depreciated and amortized will often have to be replaced in the future, and EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA do not reflect any cash requirements for such replacements, (v) they do not adjust for all non-cash income or expense items that are reflected in our statements of cash flows, (vi) they do not reflect the impact of earnings or charges resulting from matters we consider not to be indicative of our on-going operations, and (vii) other companies in our industry may calculate these measures differently than we do, limiting their usefulness as comparative measures. We compensate for these limitations by providing specific information regarding the GAAP amounts excluded from such non-GAAP financial measures. We further compensate for the limitations in our use of non-GAAP financial measures by presenting comparable GAAP measures more prominently. Management believes that EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA facilitate operating performance comparisons from period to period by isolating the effects of some items that vary from period to period without any correlation to core operating performance or that vary widely among similar companies. These potential differences may be caused by variations in capital structures (affecting interest expense), tax positions (such as the impact on periods or companies of changes in effective tax rates or NOLs) and the age and book depreciation of facilities and equipment (affecting relative depreciation expense). We also present EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA because (i) management believes that these measures are frequently used by securities analysts, investors and other interested parties to evaluate companies in our industry, (ii) management believes that investors will find these measures useful in assessing our ability to service or incur indebtedness, and (iii) we use EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA internally for a number of benchmarks, including to compare our performance to that of our competitors. Adjusted Net Income is neither required by, nor presented in accordance with, GAAP. Adjusted net income represents net income adjusted for (i) costs (or gains) related to loss (or gains) on disposal of assets and asset impairment and closed store costs reserves, (ii) expenses related to special legal and professional fees, (iii) extraordinary legal settlement costs, (iv) restructuring charges and executive transition costs, (v) insurance proceeds related to reimbursement of lost profits, net of the related costs and (vi) provision for income taxes at a normalized tax rate of 28.5% and 28.8% for the thirteen and twenty-six weeks ended July 1, 2026, respectively, and 29.3% for both the thirteen and twenty-six weeks ended June 25, 2025 which reflects our estimated long-term effective tax rate, including both federal and state income taxes (excluding the impact of discrete items) and applied after giving effect to the foregoing adjustments. Because other companies may calculate these measures differently than we do, adjusted net income as presented herein may not be comparable to similarly titled measures reported by other companies. Management believes adjusted net income is an important supplement to GAAP measures that enhances the overall understanding of our operating performance and long-term profitability, and enables investors to more effectively compare the Company’s performance to prior and future periods. title: [Toyota Times] Tateshina Meeting: Uniting Industries for Zero Traffic Accidents
summary: This year's Tateshina Meeting once again brought together leaders from across industries to discuss how to achieve zero traffic accidents. Participants looked back on the origins of Shoko-ji Temple and reaffirmed their resolve to build a safer society. #TOYOTATIMES
body_text: This year's Tateshina Meeting once again brought together leaders from across industries to discuss how to achieve zero traffic accidents. Participants looked back on the origins of Shoko-ji Temple and reaffirmed their resolve to build a safer society. 2,547 people. That's how many lost their lives in traffic accidents in Japan in 2025, according to figures released by the National Police Agency. It is the lowest figure since record-keeping began in 1948, though the rate of decline has slowed in recent years. Leaders from across industries once again came together at this year's Tateshina Meeting, united in their commitment to achieving zero traffic accidents. This year's meeting began by looking back on the origins of Mount Tateshina Shoko-ji Temple (Chino City, Nagano Prefecture), where the summer festival was held on July 17. In 1970, when annual traffic deaths topped 16,000 in what came to be known as the "Traffic War," Shoko-ji Temple was built as a place to pray for traffic safety and remember the victims of accidents. Participants once again took to heart the commitment of those who worked to establish the temple. ITS* was a topic of discussion for achieving safer traffic through a "three-pronged approach" focusing on people, cars, and infrastructure. Executive Vice President Hiroki Nakajima, Toyota Research Institute CEO Gill Pratt, and others discussed its benefits and challenges. *Intelligent Transport Systems (ITS): systems that connect people, cars, and roads through communication technology, enabling the exchange of information that vehicles alone cannot obtain to support safer driving. This year's Tateshina Meeting once again featured a wide range of organizations sharing their efforts, spanning automobiles, bicycles, telecommunications, universities, and more. The words "together" and "united" were heard frequently in the participants’ reports. Behind these words was the same resolve: to come together and end these tragic accidents. Since 2023, the Tateshina Meeting has also organized subcommittee activities to make its traffic safety initiatives more effective. After this year's meeting, an app that helps parents and children learn about traffic safety on school routes together was also unveiled as part of efforts to raise safety awareness among children. facebook X（formerly Twitter）

title: Understanding the hidden risks of generic parts in crane maintenance
summary: They might appear to be a good alternative to OEM originals, but counterfeit or generic parts are often manufactured without adhering to the rigorous specifications and quality standards set by the original equipment manufacturer.Generic components often require more frequent servicing or replacement, eroding initial cost savings and increasing downtime.The use of non-original components can invalidate regional certifications or warranties, exposing crane owners to legal and financial risk, and workers to safety risks.
body_text: Half price, half lifespan Because generics are typically manufactured with lower-grade materials to reduce costs, their lifespan is often significantly shorter than genuine parts. This means they must be serviced or replaced more frequently, eroding initial savings, increasing downtime, and potentially endangering the jobsite. In many cases, opting for a cheaper alternative does not make financial sense in the long-term, and introduces additional risk for owners. “As a manufacturer, it is in Manitowoc’s interest to maintain the high value of our equipment,” said Yannick Richaud. “Generic parts can cause premature wear of other components because they are built by companies that do not fully understand the overall specifications of a crane or are solely focused on profit. At Manitowoc, we engineer our cranes to offer reduced maintenance frequency, limited wear of components, and minimized downtime. Introducing non-OEM parts into these cranes puts the long-term performance and value of a crane at risk.” Real consequences Beyond operational risks, generic parts can expose crane owners to additional consequences. One of the most critical considerations is the loss of manufacturer support. Load charts for Grove, Manitowoc, and Potain cranes are invalidated when non-OEM components are used. If a structural component is repaired in an unknown way; or an OEM component is replaced with a generic component, the load chart for the crane is no longer valid. It’s worth keeping in mind that while some generic parts suppliers may offer limited warranties, these typically cover only the part itself, not any resulting damage to the crane. Additionally, the use of non-original components will invalidate regional certifications and OEM warranties. In practical terms, that means operators and crane owners could be held responsible, even if a relatively inexpensive non-original component causes extensive downstream damage. Genuine parts, on the other hand, allow crane owners to benefit from high-quality technical support, helping maximize uptime and protect the long-term value of the equipment. A growing global problem The issue of generic parts is especially prevalent in regions with limited regulatory oversight or where enforcement of safety and material quality standards is less stringent. Manitowoc and other manufacturers have identified generic versions of all kinds of components, from small parts to complex structural elements like mast sections for tower cranes or jib extensions for mobile cranes. “Manitowoc views the reliable operation and productivity of its cranes as essential pillars to project success. Cutting corners on critical components is a risk no crane owner or operator should ever take,” Richaud said. title: New Importer of Record Rules Could Reshape Customs and Tax Planning for Foreign Companies
summary: New importer of record rules may raise customs, tax, transfer pricing, and nexus risks for foreign companies importing goods into the U.S.
body_text: Foreign companies that import goods into the United States may need to revisit their customs and tax structures before new importer of record (IOR) rules take effect. A June 3, 2026, executive order directs the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to strengthen customs enforcement, with a focus on IOR accountability, duty collection, supply chain transparency, and enforcement against undervaluation, misclassification, forced labor, and illegal transshipment. Although the order is framed as a customs enforcement measure, the business impact may reach well beyond entry documentation. Foreign importers should assess how the new requirements could affect customs compliance, federal income tax exposure, transfer pricing, state and local tax nexus, cash flow, and supply chain operations. What Is Changing? The executive order requires federal agencies to revise rules, guidance, and policies governing IOR eligibility. Those revisions are expected to include minimum domestic asset or bonding requirements, greater bond coverage, additional reporting to CBP, and expanded disclosures involving anticipated import volumes, ownership, beneficial ownership, business affiliations, and domestic assets. The order also targets foreign IORs that use informal entry processes for low-value imports. CBP is directed to prohibit foreign IORs from filing informal entries and to impose additional formal entry requirements. For formal entries, foreign IORs may be restricted from relying on continuous bonds unless CBP determines that revenue is fully protected and compliance can be assured. They also may need to be validated through the Customs Trade Partnership Against Terrorism (CTPAT) program, if eligible, or use a CTPAT-validated licensed customs broker. The order further instructs CBP to update the IOR registry, remove inactive IORs, confirm active IOR compliance, create risk-based tiers, and establish enhanced vetting for parties involved in import activity. Customs Risks Are Expected to Rise The compliance standard for importers is already significant. Under 19 U.S.C. § 1484, an importer of record must use reasonable care when filing the documentation or information needed for CBP to determine release, value, classification, duty rate, statistics, and other legal requirements. The executive order raises the stakes by directing agencies to increase audits, enforce liquidated damages claims, restrict in-bond use, and impose maximum penalties on brokers in certain circumstances. It also calls for revised mitigation standards, including a minimum penalty floor of not less than 50% of the assessed penalty, absent exceptional circumstances that materially affect national security. Those requirements matter because 19 U.S.C. § 1592 already prohibits fraudulent, grossly negligent, or negligent statements or omissions in connection with importing merchandise into U.S. commerce. Penalties can vary by level of culpability and, in cases of fraud, may reach the domestic value of the merchandise. For importers, the practical risk is clear: documentation gaps, classification errors, unsupported valuations, or inconsistent origin claims may become more expensive and harder to resolve. The Tax Consequences May Be Even More Significant Foreign companies may respond to the new IOR standards by expanding their U.S. footprint through assets, personnel, affiliates, or operating structures. Those changes may help satisfy customs requirements, but they can also create U.S. tax implications. The IRS explains that when a foreign person engages in a U.S. trade or business, U.S.-source income connected with that business is generally treated as effectively connected income (ECI). ECI is taxed in the U.S. on a net basis at graduated rates after allowable deductions. By contrast, certain fixed, determinable, annual, or periodical income that is not ECI may be subject to a 30% tax rate, or a lower treaty rate, on the gross amount. State and local tax exposure also deserves attention. CBIZ guidance notes that nexus is the connection between a taxpayer and a state that creates a filing obligation. Activities such as physical presence, employees, inventory, or reaching sales thresholds may establish nexus. Since South Dakota v. Wayfair, states have expanded economic nexus standards, particularly for sales tax collection. Transfer pricing is another pressure point. If customs values, related-party pricing, and income tax positions are not aligned, companies may face more questions from customs and tax authorities. Importers should consider whether their documentation supports both customs and tax reporting positions. Actions to Consider Before the December 2026 Deadline Companies importing goods into the U.S. should begin planning across customs, tax, finance, and operations: Review current IOR structures and identifying whether a foreign IOR model remains practical Assess bond coverage, domestic asset needs, broker relationships, and CTPAT-related requirements Test classification, valuation, country-of-origin, and supply chain documentation Review related-party import pricing for consistency across customs and income tax reporting Evaluate whether U.S. assets, personnel, or affiliates could create ECI or state and local tax nexus Model cash flow impacts from higher duties, bonding requirements, technology investments, and advisory costs Update record retention and internal controls before enforcement deadlines arrive Looking Ahead The executive order could make importer of record planning a broader business issue for foreign companies selling into the U.S. Customs compliance, tax structure, transfer pricing, and state nexus should be reviewed together rather than handled as separate workstreams. Companies that act early may be better positioned to preserve market access, manage duty and penalty exposure, and avoid creating unintended tax obligations. Those that wait may face a more complicated restructuring process after the new enforcement framework takes effect. If you have questions about the executive order, please contact a member of our international tax team . Frequently Asked Questions A June 3, 2026, executive order directs federal agencies to strengthen IOR eligibility requirements, customs enforcement, reporting obligations, bond requirements, and importer vetting processes. Foreign importers may face increased reporting requirements, higher bonding obligations, enhanced compliance scrutiny, and additional restrictions on entry processes. Potentially. Foreign companies that expand their U.S. presence through assets, personnel, affiliates, or operating structures to meet IOR requirements may create U.S. federal income tax or state and local tax obligations. Customs valuations, related-party pricing, and income tax reporting positions should align. Inconsistencies can increase scrutiny from both customs and tax authorities. Companies should review their IOR structure, assess bond and reporting requirements, test customs documentation, evaluate tax nexus risks, review transfer pricing policies, and strengthen internal controls before enforcement begins. © Copyright CBIZ, Inc. title: Living shoreline restoration reaches new milestone along the Elizabeth River
body_text: Norfolk Southern has completed the final phase of its Living Shoreline restoration project at Lamberts Point, a nature-based effort along the Elizabeth River that transformed nearly nine acres and 1,500 feet of eroded shoreline. Using native vegetation, oyster habitat, and other natural features, the project improves water quality, restores wildlife habitat, and helps protect critical rail infrastructure. Developed in partnership with the Elizabeth River Project , the award-winning restoration replaces traditional stone barriers with a living shoreline that works with nature to stabilize the coast, strengthen the surrounding ecosystem, and improve the health of the river. Why it matters : Coastal erosion threatens shorelines and waterways across the country. The Living Shoreline demonstrates how working with nature can restore vulnerable coastlines while creating lasting environmental and community benefits. Building a more resilient shoreline The Living Shoreline builds on a more than 30-year partnership between Norfolk Southern and the Elizabeth River Project. The final restoration phase, completed in May, included planting 173 trees, 192 shrubs, and native marsh grasses across the site. An ongoing oyster gardening initiative also raises and places approximately 6,000 young oysters each year on offshore reef structures to enhance the habitat and improve water quality. In addition, the project recently marked one year since its first nutrient credit release , which has supported more than 140 credit transactions. Earned by voluntarily reducing nutrients entering the river, the credits help local industries and municipalities meet their environmental obligations while demonstrating how environmental restoration can create lasting economic value. The completed Living Shoreline at Lamberts Point reflects years of restoration efforts along the Elizabeth River, helping protect critical infrastructure and surrounding ecosystems. The completed Living Shoreline at Lamberts Point reflects years of restoration efforts along the Elizabeth River, helping protect critical infrastructure and surrounding ecosystems. The completed Living Shoreline at Lamberts Point reflects years of restoration efforts along the Elizabeth River, helping protect critical infrastructure and surrounding ecosystems. What they're saying “Norfolk Southern's Living Shoreline is a remarkable example of how environmental restoration and industrial operations can work hand in hand. It demonstrates that investing in our natural resources not only benefits the river and surrounding wildlife but also makes strong business sense. Over the years, I've seen firsthand the impact that committed partners can have on the health of this watershed, and Norfolk Southern's leadership continues to set an example for others to follow.” – Pam Boatwright, Deputy Director & River Star Businesses Manager, Elizabeth River Project What we're saying "The Living Shoreline at Lamberts Point shows what's possible when organizations come together around a shared commitment to protecting our communities and natural resources. Together with the Elizabeth River Project, we're protecting critical infrastructure, improving the health of the river, and creating lasting environmental and economic benefits for years to come." — Josh Raglin, Chief Sustainability Officer, Norfolk Southern The power of partnership The Living Shoreline serves as a model for how businesses, nonprofit organizations, and local stakeholders can work together to address local environmental challenges. By combining Norfolk Southern’s resources and long-term presence in the region with the Elizabeth River Project’s expertise, the partnership delivered a solution tailored to the unique needs of the Elizabeth River and the surrounding community. The project demonstrates how long-term collaboration can turn shared priorities into practical, sustainable solutions. Learn more about NS’ sustainability commitment in the 2026 Forging a Better Tomorrow report .

title: Kyndryl introduces new agentic modernization services-as-software scaled through Kyndryl Bridge
summary: Kyndryl introduces Agentic Modernization services-as-software to help businesses accelerate modernization, reduce risk and scale AI.
body_text: Codifies decades of Kyndryl engineering expertise into agentic workflows that help enterprises accelerate modernization, reduce risk and maximize business agility Trusted by more than 1,400 customers, Kyndryl Bridge provides the technology foundation to deploy, orchestrate and govern agentic workflows and AI agents across IT estates NEW YORK, August 6, 2026 — Kyndryl (NYSE: KD), a leading provider of mission-critical enterprise technology services, today introduced its Agentic Modernization services-as-software, which is built using the Kyndryl Agentic AI Framework and is scaled through Kyndryl Bridge . Services-as-software is an emerging model for delivering services through software-driven automation, intelligence and scalable digital workflows. Kyndryl has codified its trusted mission-critical and engineering expertise, together with capabilities from AI ecosystem partners, into pre-defined agentic workflows that help customers unlock business outcomes, de-risk and accelerate their modernization objectives, while maintaining enterprise guardrails and cost visibility throughout their AI adoption journey. “Modernization is becoming an operating discipline rather than a series of labor-intensive transformation programs that are difficult to scale and disruption-prone," said Ismail Amla, Senior Vice President, Kyndryl Consult. “As technology innovation accelerates exponentially, organizations need to move toward continuous modernization so they can adapt faster to changing business needs. With Agentic Modernization services-as-software, customers can transform iteratively and seamlessly using proven agentic workflows designed to handle changing business priorities and built on Kyndryl’s deep mission-critical expertise and industrialized through Kyndryl Bridge, enabling faster execution and more predictable outcomes.” The announcement comes as organizations race to scale AI but are challenged to achieve business value from their investments. Kyndryl’s recent survey of 1,100 business and technology leaders found that while 77% of executives say generative AI has already been scaled across multiple functions of their organization, only 32% report experiencing one of their top desired outcomes. Organizations cannot reliably adopt AI on aging technology estates; modernization is the prerequisite foundation and has become a top priority and a growing area of technology spend. “Agentic AI is reshaping how enterprises think about modernization, moving the conversation from large, episodic transformation projects to continuous, agent-orchestrated implementations guided by human expertise,” said Bill Latshaw, Research Director, Worldwide Business Consulting Services, IDC. “Kyndryl’s Agentic Modernization services-as-software, with Kyndryl Bridge as the foundation, reflects that shift, combining pre-defined AI workflows and operational expertise, critically with the governance and guardrails needed to enable organizations to modernize with greater speed and consistency by reducing indecision and complexity traps.” Run on the Foundation of Kyndryl Bridge Since its launch in 2022, Kyndryl Bridge has become the trusted foundation for managing and modernizing mission-critical and regulated technology environments for more than 1,400 customers. Kyndryl Bridge generates more than 16 million AI insights each month and has demonstrated a reduction in IT incidents by up to 50%. As organizations adopt AI-powered workflows, Kyndryl Bridge serves as the robust enterprise-grade technology foundation, for deploying and managing mission-critical AI across hybrid IT estates, with well-established controls for cost visibility, security and regulatory requirements. Kyndryl Bridge also provides agentic memory management for customers, helping them preserve and evolve critical institutional knowledge and operational context to support continuous modernization. Scaling modernization outcomes with services-as-software Kyndryl’s services-as-software helps customers execute modernization programs of any size or complexity in radically compressed timelines and at significantly lower cost by scaling pre-built agentic workflows — making specialized skills less of a constraint. This approach also enables customers to adopt new frontier models and tools as they become available, based on their business requirements, cost, performance and governance needs, without locking them into a specific technology stack. As a result, modernization programs can be delivered with greater consistency, repeatability, quality and predictable outcomes for every customer. Expert-guided, agent-orchestrated continuous modernization Anchored in Kyndryl’s decades of experience managing and modernizing mission-critical systems, pre-defined enterprise-grade agentic modernization workflows support a broad range of infrastructure, application and business transformation initiatives across distributed and mainframe environments, public, private cloud and network infrastructure, software development and IT operations. These AI workflows orchestrate autonomous AI agents across the modernization lifecycle, helping accelerate activities such as discovery, code analysis, dependency mapping, target-state design, code generation, testing and validation. Kyndryl’s pre-defined agentic modernization workflows also reduce the effort and costs required to experiment with AI and accelerate modernization by giving customers a proven, reusable foundation for generating consistent, high-quality outcomes at scale. Kyndryl experts and customer teams remain central to the process, providing human oversight, governance and accountability. With Kyndryl’s Agentic Modernization services-as-software, organizations can transform legacy environments faster and more consistently, into modern, AI-ready environments with greater speed and confidence. Customers are already seeing results: A global car rental company is transforming its software development lifecycle with Kyndryl AI agents, autonomously refactoring legacy code and reducing hours of manual effort to minutes while improving code quality, consistency and maintainability. At a global reinsurer, the starting point was a decades-old mainframe environment with millions of lines of code and a shrinking pool of in-house expertise. Kyndryl Agentic Modernization services-as-software helped analyze and reimagine the legacy estate, accelerating the transition to a cloud-native architecture and enabling data center exit timelines to be reduced by 50%. A global financial services organization has deployed Kyndryl Agentic Modernization services-as-software across its engineering teams worldwide to accelerate modernization using AI-powered operational insights and pre-defined agentic workflows. body_text: News Details View all news Revvity Launches SuperFlex Prenatal Screening System, Expanding Access to Preeclampsia Testing 08/10/2026 Download this Press Release (opens in new window) PDF 99 KB Revvity’s new maternal and fetal biochemistry testing platform Designed for accessibility, simplicity, and flexibility Purpose-built for small to mid-sized labs and clinics to enable this capability in-house for the first time WALTHAM, Mass. — August 10, 2026 — Revvity, Inc. today announced the launch of the SuperFlex™ prenatal screening system , a compact, CE-IVDR certified immunoassay instrument designed to bring high-quality screening to laboratories and clinics seeking reliable, rapid solutions that fit lower-volume workflows. The system supports testing for preeclampsia, a condition that affects between 2% and 8% of pregnancies and is increasing globally due to rising maternal age and conditions such as diabetes and hypertension. Despite international guidelines recommending screening, access has historically been limited to high-throughput centralized laboratories. SuperFlex addresses these gaps by delivering three core advantages: Accessible entry — affordable instrument cost with just one annual maintenance, and no reagent wastage even when sample volumes are low Operational simplicity — a user-friendly design that minimizes training requirements, to be seamlessly integrated with Revvity’s LifeCycle™ software for streamlined risk assessment and LIMS data transfer Flexible throughput — continuous sample loading delivers results in as little as 14 minutes per test, accommodating both urgent and routine workflows "This SuperFlex offering represents a significant addition to our prenatal portfolio," said Anna Godenhjelm, vice president and general manager of reproductive health at Revvity. "By removing the financial and operational barriers to in-house prenatal screening, we are giving more women access to potentially life-saving testing regardless of where they receive care." The platform also includes a test menu for both first- and second-trimester biochemical prenatal screening, enabling a versatile, cost-effective, random-access solution well-suited for decentralized testing. The SuperFlex platform will initially be available in all markets that accept CE-marked instruments, with expansion into Asia-Pacific planned for late 2026. title: Examining Human-Like Behaviors in LLMs: A Multi-Dimensional Analysis of Model Behaviors, User Factors, and System Prompts
summary: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit a wide range of human-like behaviors, from expressing thoughts and emotions, to engaging in…
body_text: View publication Large language models (LLMs) exhibit a wide range of human-like behaviors, from expressing thoughts and emotions, to engaging in relationship-building with users, to refusing requests and maintaining boundaries. Despite their prevalence, researchers and practitioners lack methods and empirical insights to make informed decisions about when and what types of human-like behaviors LLMs should exhibit. To fill this gap, we present a multi-dimensional analysis of the prevalence, potential effects, and controllability of these behaviors using LLM-as-a-judge and human evaluation. Across 21,000 multi-turn conversations from four widely used models (gpt-4o, gpt-4.1-mini, claude-sonnet-4.6, gemini-2.5-flash), we find that human-like behaviors are pervasive but vary across models and user factors (conversation goals and user profiles). In terms of perceived appropriateness, human evaluators judged self-referential and relationship-building behaviors as less appropriate from LLMs than from humans, but boundary-maintaining behaviors more appropriate from LLMs than from humans. Finally, we show that system prompting can control these behaviors, though it requires careful evaluation to avoid unintended effects. We discuss the implications of our findings and provide recommendations for responsible LLM design and evaluation.

title: CRM Requirements: How to Define What Your Business Actually Needs (2026 Guide)
summary: CRM requirements explained: define core needs, compare options, and control costs. Discover the impact of custom-built CRM in 2026.
body_text: TL;DR: To define CRM requirements for your business, identify your must-have workflows and data needs, prioritize features with real operational impact, and account for both upfront and ongoing costs, including flexibility to fit your future processes. CRM Requirements: How to Define What Your Business Actually Needs (2026 Guide) Last updated: August 2026 CRM buyers in 2026 face more options than ever, from off-the-shelf tools to highly customizable platforms. Rising subscription costs and rigid templates have left many teams with systems that don't fit their actual workflows. Driving both inefficiency and wasted spend. New custom CRM solutions now let businesses align requirements directly to processes while controlling costs, shifting the conversation from checkbox features to real operational value. What are CRM requirements, and why do they determine real value? CRM requirements are the concrete functions, data structures, and workflows your business needs to serve customers efficiently. The more precisely you define these needs, the less likely you are to overpay for features you never use or struggle with a CRM that forces process workarounds. Most teams skip this step, ending up with generic, bloated systems that create hidden costs. By getting requirements right up front, before vendor selection, you ensure technology fits your operation, not the other way around. This is where many off-the-shelf platforms (including well-known names like Insightly and Salesforce) fall short for teams with specialized needs, driving up both financial and process costs. How to identify and map your CRM requirements Accurately mapping your CRM requirements begins with a clear process: document your sales, marketing, and service workflows as they exist today, catalog the essential customer data and touchpoints to track, map out which roles need what access, and rank each workflow by importance. Only then can you distinguish true must-haves from optional automations. This upfront clarity is what enables businesses to avoid feature bloat and make informed CRM decisions that actually fit their processes. The first step is rigorous documentation of your existing workflows across all customer-facing functions. Chart out each process for sales (such as lead capture, qualification, quoting, closing), marketing (campaign planning, nurture tracks, event invites), and support or service (ticketing, escalation paths, resolution steps). Note each decision point, approval handoff, and the tools currently in use. This creates a process map that anchors your CRM wish-list in current reality, not just future ambitions. Next, list the specific data fields and touchpoints you need to track for each customer. For instance, sales teams might require fields like lead source, deal value, industry, and key contact roles, while customer service could need ticket history, satisfaction ratings, and renewal dates. Map out every touchpoint, phone calls, emails, demo requests, or support tickets, that should create or update a CRM record. For more on structuring data for actionable insights, see CRM Database Strategies for 2026: 9 Ways to Build, Use, and Optimize Customer Data . Role mapping brings clarity to permissions and reporting needs. Specify which team members require access to which records (e.g., sales reps see their own pipeline, managers oversee all deals, finance reviews won contracts), and define the kinds of custom reports or dashboards each role depends on. By aligning CRM permissions with job functions, you not only safeguard sensitive information but also ensure each user sees relevant data without unnecessary clutter, directly supporting adoption. Distinguishing between must-have workflows and nice-to-have automation keeps your requirements grounded. Must-haves are functions that, if missing, would disrupt critical processes or compliance, for example, logging every customer communication automatically or syncing opportunity stages with forecast reports. Nice-to-haves may include things like automatic meeting scheduling or drip email journeys, which add convenience but aren’t essential to your core business operations. Being ruthless in this differentiation prevents overbuying and helps clarify where customization or add-ons might be warranted. A well-developed process map serves as both a feature filter and a diagnostic tool when evaluating CRM options. It allows you to instantly spot which platforms accommodate your key flows natively, and which would force clunky workarounds or leave gaps. This systematic approach doesn’t just minimize wasted spend on unused features. It positions your organization to measure the real impact of each CRM investment. For those considering whether to seek custom development, frameworks like the ones discussed in Custom CRM Development Software Solutions: A Comprehensive Guide for 2026 can further refine the requirements gathering phase. By methodically mapping roles, data, and workflow needs before software shopping, you set the stage for a CRM that enables, not dictates, how your business succeeds. Core CRM features every business needs (and why they matter) Every business needs a CRM with six foundational features: standard contact management, opportunity or deal tracking, task assignment with activity logs, basic reporting and dashboards, and robust role-based access controls. These core functions form the minimum viable CRM stack, providing a reliable backbone for customer data and team collaboration. Regardless of industry or organizational complexity. Standard contact management is the non-negotiable starting point. This capability provides a centralized repository to store all customer, lead, and partner information. With contact management, teams avoid scattered spreadsheets and inconsistent records, enabling quick updates, unified views, and efficient communication. Robust CRMs let you segment contacts, track touchpoints, and store key details such as addresses, preferences, and account ownership. Opportunity and deal tracking comes next, allowing businesses to visualize and manage their sales pipelines. This feature lets teams define deal stages, forecast revenue, and maintain accountability for follow-ups. By tracking where each opportunity stands, you can identify bottlenecks in your sales process and spot at-risk deals early. For insight into pipeline health and sales effectiveness, deal tracking is indispensable. Task assignment and activity logging are essential for coordination and operational clarity. Assigning tasks within the CRM ensures accountability, so nothing falls through the cracks. Comprehensive activity logs, calls, emails, meetings, notes, create an audit trail and institutional memory, letting teams see the full customer history at a glance. This reduces duplicated efforts and bolsters service continuity, especially as teams grow or roles shift. Basic reporting and dashboards reshape raw data into actionable insights. Even the simplest CRM should generate standard sales, pipeline, and activity reports. Built-in dashboards offer quick overviews of key metrics. Closed-won rates, follow-up frequency, or task completion. For a deeper look at effective CRM metrics, visit 10 Essential CRM Metrics for Business Success in 2026 . Finally, role-based access and security controls protect sensitive information and keep workflows clean. Not all employees need the same level of access. A marketing user might see different data than an account executive or finance lead. Clear permission structures ensure compliance, data privacy, and process alignment, especially in organizations facing regulatory requirements or cross-team collaboration. A minimum viable CRM stack covers these essentials, giving every user what they need without unnecessary overhead. Businesses that prioritize these core features establish a strong foundation for consistent customer experiences and scalable operations, whether they custom-build or use an off-the-shelf platform. Book a call Advanced CRM features: when do you actually need them? Advanced CRM features like automation, analytics dashboards, and native integrations can dramatically extend your system’s capabilities, but each additional layer increases complexity and cost. Often without corresponding value unless they’re mapped precisely to your team’s business processes. Businesses that benefit most from advanced features are those with mature, well-defined workflows that risk bottlenecks or lost opportunities if they remain manual or fragmented. For most teams, assuming you “need” every advanced add-on leads to overbuilt, expensive CRM deployments and undetected inefficiency. Automation sits at the top of many feature wishlists: think workflow designers, rules engines, and automatic triggers for lead assignment, deal stage changes, or follow-up emails. These systems promise efficiency by minimizing manual entries and guiding users through sales or support processes. However, automation’s value depends entirely on having consistent, structured processes. Without this, automations can cement unwieldy workflows, mask process flaws, or drive up implementation and maintenance burdens as requirements shift. Email and calendar integration enables end-to-end visibility and unified scheduling. Features like auto-logging conversations, syncing meetings, and click-to-email functionality seem essential, especially for client-facing teams. Yet the hidden costs can emerge in integration stability, privacy management, and vendor lock-in, especially when your CRM requires constant syncing with multiple third-party platforms. For some organizations, manual logging or lightweight integration meets compliance and reporting needs with far less overhead. Custom dashboards and analytics are often marketed as a major advantage for data-driven decision-making. The catch: building effective dashboards demands both access to high-quality, consistent data and clear organizational KPIs. Out-of-the-box reports in most platforms cover basic needs. Extensive custom dashboards might only be justified for businesses with unique metrics or board-level reporting requirements. Sustaining customized analytics can mean IT overhead and ongoing consultant fees, complicating an area that should empower, not slow down, day-to-day operations. Teams planning KPI-driven growth can find more guidance in 10 Essential CRM Metrics for Business Success in 2026 . Native third-party integrations , with marketing automation, customer support, or ERP systems, sound like a logical way to extend the CRM’s reach. The challenge is that each “native” integration brings ongoing update cycles, potential for API changes breaking workflows, and data mapping demands as other tools evolve. Over-customizing this layer can also make future migrations more difficult, locking organizations into vendors or slowing adoption of new top software. AI features such as recommendations, predictive lead scoring, or suggested follow-ups are increasingly highlighted in CRM marketing. While these capabilities can surface hidden opportunities, they’re rarely “plug-and-play.” Real impact requires clean historical data, clear definitions of what predictions drive value, and internal readiness to act on AI-generated insights. Costs can escalate quickly if AI modules are purchased but adopted superficially, or if teams must continually adjust models to reflect industry shifts. There’s a clear trade-off: advanced features enable potential for scale and intelligence but bring escalating costs. Licensing, setup, training, and support. For most organizations, layering too many at once creates a fragile environment, especially if process documentation lags or staff aren’t fully onboarded. A sharper requirements process demands that teams challenge vendors (and themselves): Does this feature directly support a revenue goal, compliance need, or operational bottleneck? Or is it an impressive-sounding option likely to gather dust? For deeper insights on matching CRM design to real workflows, CRM Customization: Tailoring Solutions for Optimal Efficiency in 2026 details practical approaches businesses use to strike this balance. CRM requirements checklist: building your evaluation scorecard A robust CRM requirements checklist reshapes your mapped business processes into an actionable evaluation tool: begin by listing each step in your workflow, distill related system needs into clear checklist items, assign priorities, critical, helpful, or optional, and use this scorecard to objectively compare CRM solutions. By shifting from vague feature wishlists to process-driven requirements, you reduce the risk of misalignment and overspending. Translating process maps into a requirements checklist starts by reviewing each workflow you documented, whether lead capture, deal tracking, support escalation, or account management. For every function, ask what the CRM must actually do: Does your sales process require multi-stage custom pipelines? Is field-level access control necessary for data privacy? Should customer-triggered automation integrate with your billing platform? Phrase requirements as unambiguous capabilities the CRM must support, while noting where integrations, reporting, or customization is necessary. Sample checklist items include: Contacts module must support multiple custom fields per record (e.g., contract type, renewal date) Pipeline management with customizable stages and drag-and-drop reordering Email logging tied to specific deals and contacts automatically Role-based permissions: restrict financial data to management users only Reporting dashboard able to filter by rep, pipeline stage, or region One-click export of all customer activity data for compliance audits Integration with existing accounting system via API or native connector Mobile app with offline access for field sales teams Each item needs a priority: mission-critical if it’s non-negotiable for operations, helpful if it improves efficiency or insight, and optional if it’s nice-to-have or future-facing. For example, pipeline customization may be mandatory, while advanced social media integration could be flagged optional. Explicitly marking these distinctions keeps your evaluation focused on essentials. As you rank, challenge whether each item addresses a real operational need or merely follows conventional lists. Chasing features for their own sake undermines clarity and increases the risk of feature bloat. Feature bloat and checklist fatigue are two common traps. It's easy to fall into the habit of copying requirement lists from online templates or peers. Generic checklists, no matter how comprehensive, will overlook your unique workflows and inflate your CRM expectations with features you don't need. This approach not only complicates the buying process, but often leads to overpaying for underused modules. Deliberately exclude any item that doesn't map to a documented process or a specific business outcome. Turning your checklist into a vendor evaluation rubric means rewriting requirements as pass/fail or graded criteria to compare CRM options objectively. Build a table or scoring matrix where each CRM is assessed against your prioritized needs. Create weighting for must-haves versus nice-to-haves so critical business drivers cannot be overshadowed by “bonus” features. This level of structure not only protects against persuasive demos but also justifies your decisions to stakeholders. For a deeper dive on tailoring CRM features and avoiding checklist overload, see CRM Customization: Tailoring Solutions for Optimal Efficiency in 2026 . Operational consequences: What happens if you get CRM requirements wrong? Selecting a CRM platform based on poorly defined requirements leads directly to financial waste, operational bottlenecks, and diminished team effectiveness. Often in ways that remain hidden until costly to fix. The most immediate consequences include licensing fees for unused features, workflow inefficiencies caused by forced process workarounds, fractured data across incompatible systems, poor adoption rates, and expensive migration needs when the solution inevitably falls short. One of the largest hidden costs in CRM deployments comes from feature sprawl. Many teams license all-in-one platforms promising every imaginable tool, but only use a fraction of what they pay for. This is especially acute with per-seat pricing models: modules for marketing automation, customer support, or advanced analytics can remain idle, while the organization is billed for their potential rather than actual use. Over time, these unused licenses can drain budgets and reduce ROI, particularly for larger teams or those with shifting requirements. Analysis of CRM database strategies shows that unused features not only inflate subscription costs but contribute to unnecessary complexity, making onboarding and navigation slower for employees who only need specific functionality. Workflow misalignment is another costly byproduct of mismatched requirements. Generic CRMs often require teams to mold their processes around the software. Leading to clunky workarounds, manual data entry, or duplicated effort across tools. This friction chips away at productivity and can erode trust in the system itself. Employees may revert to spreadsheets or external apps, sidestepping the CRM entirely when the solution fails to reflect how they actually work. The result is a patchwork of partial adoption that undermines visibility and collaboration. Data silos emerge quickly when a chosen CRM cannot accommodate a team's unique data structures or integrations. Key information winds up trapped in disconnected tools or legacy systems, blocking the unified customer view that organizations expect from a modern CRM. These silos not only reduce reporting accuracy but make compliance and insight generation far more difficult, as discussed in our guide on CRM reporting and challenges . Team adoption and morale may suffer if the CRM feels like an imposition rather than a value add. Employees forced to use features or layouts that don’t fit their job roles can become disengaged, lowering utilization rates and amplifying the perceived burden of “yet another tool.” Over time, resistance to change can harden, making later process improvements or migrations twice as challenging. Finally, mismatched CRM systems often incur long-term costs that far exceed their upfront price tag. If the CRM’s core setup or licensing model fails to scale with your needs, or if you grow out of the platform’s limitations, switching later can involve major new investments in data migration, additional add-ons, and retraining. These transition costs rarely get factored into initial budgeting, yet they define the true total cost of ownership. A careful requirements process, centered on real workflows rather than generic checklists, is the best insurance against these expensive pitfalls. Custom CRM, off-the-shelf platform, or hybrid: which model fits your requirements? A custom CRM is the best fit for businesses with specialized processes, unique data requirements, or a strong need for infrastructure independence, while off-the-shelf SaaS CRMs like Salesforce and HubSpot suit organizations with standard workflows, rapid deployment needs, and moderate customization demands. Hybrid models, combining managed customization with elements of SaaS, are an option for teams that require more flexibility than pure SaaS offers without the commitment of a full custom build. Your mapped requirements, anticipated growth, and appetite for long-term cost control dictate which approach is optimal. Off-the-shelf SaaS CRMs appeal to companies looking for quick setup, proven reliability, and a wide array of built-in features. Popular choices like HubSpot, Salesforce, and Insightly deliver integrated sales, marketing, and support functions “out of the box.” This efficiency makes them attractive for organizations with standardized processes that map well to the defaults established by major vendors. High-quality documentation, app marketplaces, and established support channels further simplify onboarding. However, convenience comes with constraints. SaaS CRMs commonly restrict workflow customization, often forcing teams to adapt their business processes around the platform rather than molding the platform to their needs. Over time, workarounds and vendor-imposed limitations can create inefficiencies or data silos. Financially, the standard per-seat or per-feature subscription pricing leads to spiraling costs as teams grow, especially for companies with larger sales or support organizations. Custom-built CRMs suit businesses with non-standard workflows, industry-specific compliance requirements, or unique data structures. These solutions are purpose-developed to mirror an organization’s exact operations, from lead management logic to field formulas and reporting. By enabling absolute control over interface, integration, and data storage, custom CRMs eliminate the need for “sidecar” spreadsheets or patchwork integrations. They also facilitate infrastructure independence. Critical for firms prioritizing data ownership, regulatory adherence, or deploying across proprietary environments. The cost of a custom CRM tends to be front-loaded, pairing an upfront build with lower ongoing licensing (often no per-seat fees). This makes the model financially compelling for organizations facing high recurring SaaS fees resulting from large headcounts or advanced feature bundles. The critical downside is greater reliance on bespoke support and development resources, potentially slower deployment, and a higher bar for future upgrades. For a deep dive into when a custom approach is worth it, see Custom CRM Development Software Solutions: A Comprehensive Guide for 2026 . Hybrid approaches , like managed-custom solutions or modular platforms, offer a compromise: some vendors provide frameworks allowing extensive configuration without starting entirely from scratch. This caters to companies that outgrow standard SaaS but lack the appetite for greenfield development. Hybrid CRMs can deliver a balance between flexibility and reasonable implementation timelines, while still posing risks around platform lock-in and long-term maintenance. Cost structures diverge sharply across these models. Off-the-shelf SaaS options typically charge per user and per module, compounding year over year as teams expand. Custom and hybrid platforms may carry higher initial development or setup costs, but these can be offset over time by savings achieved from eliminating per-seat fees, especially for businesses with hundreds of users or highly specialized needs. Choosing the right model starts with a rigorous requirements mapping exercise. Teams should assess the gap between their processes and what SaaS platforms natively support, estimate financial impact over a realistic time horizon, and weigh future adaptability against short-term speed. The strategic fit is not just about features, but about aligning CRM delivery to support the business’s unique structure, workflows, and cost sensitivities. For many, a careful requirements-to-model comparison surfaces cost and flexibility risks early. Enabling smarter investment and smoother operations down the road. For teams in regulated industries or those managing complex data, evaluating hybrid or custom CRMs isn’t just a matter of preference. It can be essential for meeting governance, security, and compliance goals that SaaS vendors are unwilling or unable to guarantee. How to factor total cost and long-term flexibility into your CRM requirements The total cost and long-term flexibility of a CRM depend not just on upfront license fees, but on a careful reckoning of hidden costs (like user-based pricing, paid add-ons, migration expenses) and your system’s ability to adapt as your business changes. Focusing your requirements definition on both full lifecycle costs and adaptability can help you avoid cost sprawl, reduce operational risk, and minimize the likelihood of disruptive migrations down the line. Most SaaS CRM platforms rely on user-based pricing, charging a recurring fee for every team member who needs access. While this model appears simple, it often drives up costs unexpectedly as your organization grows or you expand CRM usage to new departments. Each new hire, or just an operational change that requires more logins, can lead to a sharp increase in recurring expenses. On top of seat fees, SaaS vendors typically monetize essential features as paid add-ons. Think advanced reporting, integrations, or automation. This approach can turn an affordable base plan into an expensive, sprawling stack as your use case matures. To expose the real economics, calculate the total cost of ownership for each CRM option, factoring in every cost center. This includes: Monthly or annual subscription fees for all required users and add-ons One-time or ongoing costs for data migration Fees for integrations with existing tools or systems Increases for exceeding storage or usage caps Internal costs for administration, user training, and process workarounds Indirect or hidden costs add up. For example, limitations in workflow customization can force teams into manual workarounds, reducing productivity and creating shadow IT expenses that don’t show up in basic pricing comparisons. Teams that overlook these downstream expenses may face budget overruns and surprises after going live. For a broader view of CRM cost structures, see Most Effective CRM Tools for B2B Companies in 2026: Honest Comparison . Flexibility is another foundational requirement. As your business evolves, adapting sales processes, integrating new channels, or restructuring teams, a CRM that’s rigid or heavily vendor-locked can restrict your ability to respond. Systems that only allow limited customization or tie critical data to their own infrastructure can demand expensive custom work or even force a future migration. The operational risk of inflexible, vendor-dependent CRMs becomes acute when you face a change that your platform simply can’t accommodate without major cost or disruption. By contrast, defining requirements with a clear eye toward long-term adaptability, such as open data access, workflow customizability, and infrastructure independence, not only positions your CRM to support immediate needs but guards against expensive overhauls as strategy shifts. Well-aligned requirements, including explicit needs for scalability and process fit, reduce the likelihood that you’ll need a costly migration just a few years later. To learn how custom CRM development can address these needs head-on, see our comprehensive guide . Finally, factoring total cost and flexibility into your requirements isn’t just about minimizing today’s spend. It acts as a safeguard against operational risk, lost productivity, and future costs that are often missed when buyers focus only on upfront features or sticker price. Strategic requirements definition enables informed decisions. Laying the groundwork for a CRM investment that delivers sustainable value as your business grows and adapts. Addressing data migration and integration requirements A CRM’s ability to successfully migrate legacy data and integrate with existing business systems is non-negotiable: thorough data migration prevents loss of critical customer history, while strong integration connects the CRM to tools like ERP, marketing automation, support, and analytics platforms central to daily operations. Failing to define these technical requirements alongside your business needs risks data silos, manual workarounds, and, at worst, broken business processes that undercut CRM ROI. The first step is to create an inventory of your current data assets. Catalog every source containing vital customer, deal, support, and financial data, including legacy CRMs, spreadsheets, ticketing tools, marketing databases, and proprietary systems. Evaluate data quality, identify duplicates or inconsistencies, and flag sensitive fields needing careful handling. Understanding precisely what must migrate (and in which format) directly impacts both the migration timeline and downstream business continuity. Next, map potential integration points by tracing the flow of information across your business stack. Most organizations rely on a network of operational tools: ERP for order management and invoicing, marketing platforms for campaign automation, help desk solutions for support, and analytics tools for reporting and insights. Outline not just which subsystems need to push or pull data to/from your CRM, but also the expected cadence (real-time, daily sync, or ad hoc export). Gaps here often force teams back to manual exporting or scripting. Hardly the strategic leap expected from a CRM upgrade. The consequences of missing or incomplete migrations are severe. Data loss or failed restructuring can sever continuity with long-standing clients, disrupt sales cycles, and destroy trust in the new system. Similarly, missing integration pipelines lead to redundancies or blind spots. For instance, without proper two-way sync between marketing lists and CRM records, sales teams might act on outdated leads or lose sight of ongoing campaigns. Compromising pipeline health and reporting accuracy. These topics are explored in more detail in CRM Database Strategies for 2026: 9 Ways to Build, Use, and Optimize Customer Data . Technical priorities cannot be set in isolation from business needs. Teams must weigh which integrations are mission-critical, and which can wait, and define requirements for security, scalability, and compliance. Documenting both non-negotiable needs (such as a full migration of deal history, or robust ERP-CRM connectivity) and “future nice-to-haves” guides the selection of both product and implementation plan. Lastly, ensure that your CRM plan addresses not just the launch phase, but ongoing support as your systems evolve. As your business adds new software, automates more workflows, or expands internationally, integration and data structures will need to adapt. Neglecting long-term technical flexibility often results in project fatigue and increased costs for retroactive fixes. For organizations seeking more control, custom CRM solutions outlined in Custom CRM Development Software Solutions: A Comprehensive Guide for 2026 may provide the infrastructure adaptability that off-the-shelf products struggle to offer at scale. Getting buy-in: how to align stakeholders on CRM requirements before purchase A successful CRM requirements process hinges on cross-functional alignment: key stakeholders from every department that will use or be impacted by the system must participate in both requirements gathering and final sign-off. This should always include sales, customer service, IT, and executive leadership. Excluding any group can lead to costly process gaps or future resistance. Instead of letting a single function drive the process, structure input around real business workflows to reveal needs that might otherwise go unheard. Running interactive workshops or process review sessions encourages honest, specific feedback from all involved. Invite representatives to map their day-to-day tasks and pain points, and prompt them to surface both their must-haves and wish-list features. Direct discussion often uncovers issues, like data silos or manual handoffs, that wouldn’t surface in a static requirements doc. For companies considering custom CRM development, these sessions are especially vital, as they define the foundation for any future automation or tailored interface. Conflicting priorities are inevitable: sales teams may crave advanced pipeline features, customer service might push for robust ticketing or rapid lookups, IT will focus on system security and integration, and executives often demand comprehensive reporting. To reconcile divergent needs, facilitate structured debates with transparency about technical and budgetary constraints. Prioritize features that deliver clear business value or address recurring workflow blockers. Where tradeoffs must be made, document the rationale so every stakeholder understands not just what made the list, but why other items were deferred. One of the biggest pitfalls in gathering CRM requirements is over-weighting flashy features, like AI automation, predictive lead scoring, or dashboard visualizations, at the expense of basic process fit. Under pressure from software demos or trend-based articles, teams can lose sight of their actual pain points. Anchor your process in current workflows first, and question whether each requested feature will be used in practice or become shelfware. For further insight into balancing customization with usability, see CRM Customization: Tailoring Solutions for Optimal Efficiency in 2026 . Finally, align expectations for post-launch feedback and iteration. The most accurate requirements lists are still hypotheses until the CRM encounters real usage. Commit to a formal review window, typically after the first 30 or 90 days, where every department can report what’s working and where friction remains. Build in mechanisms for ongoing adjustment, whether through configuration tweaks or development sprints, so the CRM evolves in lockstep with your processes. Ignoring post-launch feedback risks embedding inefficiencies that compound over time, undermining both user engagement and ROI. Where most CRM requirements guides fall short: cost reduction and process fit Most CRM requirements guides miss the mark by treating feature checklists as a one-size-fits-all solution. While ignoring the very real financial impact of unused features and the operational risks of forcing teams into rigid workflows. By failing to tie CRM requirements back to actual business costs and workflow alignment, many standard resources leave organizations exposed to persistent overspending and inefficiencies that only surface after implementation. A common pitfall is the assumption that "more features equals more value," which leads teams to buy CRMs packed with capabilities they’ll never touch. For example, businesses often commit to subscriptions with advanced marketing automation, integrated calling, or analytics modules simply because they're included at a certain tier, not because these tools fit their strategy. This can result in teams paying for functionalities that remain unused, while still grappling with workarounds for their unique processes. Over time, these overlooked mismatches stack up in the form of higher license fees, administration headaches, and ongoing costs that drain budgets with little operational return. Neglecting the need for custom workflow alignment can also introduce hidden costs that far exceed baseline subscription fees. Off-the-shelf CRMs typically reflect a generic “ideal” workflow, requiring teams to adjust their processes or invest in manual workarounds. For organizations with complex or highly specialized operations, this misalignment stalls adoption, increases onboarding friction, and multiplies the likelihood of data inaccuracies. Critical activities end up tracked outside the CRM. Diluting both the value of the system and the business’s visibility into performance. The essential shift is to view CRM requirements as direct levers for both cost control and adaptability. By mapping out actual processes and focusing requirement definition on what the business truly needs, organizations can sidestep surplus costs and resist vendor lock-in. This approach links every CRM line item to real operational impact: the closer the system fits the team's workflow, the greater the savings on unnecessary licenses, bolt-ons, and custom patchwork. Process mapping isn’t a tedious compliance task. It’s a strategic exercise that connects technology choices to measurable operational efficiency. Ignoring this step relegates teams to paying premiums for features that don’t fit and processes that never quite line up, undermining the promise of CRM ROI from day one. Detailed mapping is essential to avoid costly mismatches and support unique needs. For organizations at this crossroads, the priority moves beyond feature checklists. The path forward starts with an honest requirements mapping exercise: document every process, pain point, and business rule that touches the CRM. Use that map to evaluate not just surface features, but a system’s true ability to support your unique operations, whether that means considering custom CRM options (as explored in this guide ), re-assessing cost structure, or benchmarking new vendors for future flexibility. A meticulous approach here is more likely to produce a CRM that returns value across the organization, rather than introducing new inefficiencies.
